edition.copy_text: Koetschau, GCS 2–3 (1899), via the Perseus TEI

source_text: Τὸ δὲ μὴ ἐξεῖναι δουλεύειν τὸν ἀπὸ τῶν αὐτῶν ὁρμώμενον δογμάτων πλεῖον ἐτῶν ἓξ πῶς ἐστι λελογισμένον καὶ οὔτε τὸν δεσπότην οὔτε τὸν δοῦλον ἀδικοῦν, τί χρὴ λέγειν; οὐ κατὰ τὰ αὐτὰ οὖν τοῖς λοιποῖς ἔθνεσι περιστέλλοιεν ἂν Ἰουδαῖοι τὸν ἴδιον νόμον. μεμπτὸν γάρ ἐστιν αὐτοῖς καὶ ἀναισθησίας ἔγκλημα ἐπάγον τῆς περὶ τῆς τῶν νόμων ὑπεροχῆς. εἰ νομίζοιεν αὐτοὺς ὁμοίως τοῖς ἄλλοις γεγράφθαι τοῖς κατὰ τὰ ἔθνη. κἂν μὴ βούληται δὲ Κέλσος, σοφώτερόν τι εἰσὶν εἰδότες Ἰουδαῖοι οὐ μόνον τῶν πολλῶν ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν φιλοσοφεῖν δοκούντων. ὅτι οἱ μὲν φιλοσοφοῦντες μετὰ τοὺς σεμνοὺς ἐν φιλοσοφίᾳ λόγους καταπίπτουσιν ἐπὶ τὰ εἴδωλα καὶ τοὺς δαίμονας, Ἰουδαίων δὲ καὶ ὁ ἔσχατος μόνῳ ἐνορᾷ τῷ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεῷ· καὶ καλῶς γε ὅσον ἐπὶ τούτῳ σεμνύνονται καὶ τὴν τῶν ἄλλων ὡς ἐναγῶν καὶ ἀσεβῶν ἐκτρέπονται κοινωνίαν. καὶ εἴθε αὐτοῖς μὴ ἡμάρτητο παρανομήσασι καὶ πρότερον μὲν „τοὺς προφήτας“ ἀποκτείνασιν ὕστερον δὲ καὶ τῷ Ἰησοῦ ἐπιβουλεύσασιν· ἵν᾿ ἔχωμεν παράδειγμα πόλεως οὐρανίας, ἣν ἐζήτησε μὲν διαγράψαι καὶ Πλάτων οὐκ οἶδα δὲ εἰ τοσοῦτον δεδύνηται, ὅσον Μωϋσῆς ἴσχυσε καὶ οἱ μετ᾿ αὐτὸν, „γένος τι ἐκλεκτὸν“ καὶ „ἔθνος ἅγιον“ καὶ θεῷ ἀνακείμενον ἐντρέφοντες λόγοις καθαροῖς ἀπὸ πάσης δεισιδαιμονίας.
thought_title: A pattern of the heavenly city
pass_a_gloss: And the not being permitted for one setting out from the same doctrines to be a slave more than six years, how it is reasoned and wrongs neither the master nor the slave, what need is there to say? Not according to the same things then as the remaining nations would the Jews guard their own law. For it is blameworthy for them and bringing on a charge of insensibility concerning the superiority of the laws, if they should think them written similarly to the others, those according to the nations. And even if Celsus does not wish, the Jews are knowing something wiser not only than the many but also than those seeming to philosophise. Because the philosophising ones, after the august discourses in philosophy, fall down onto the idols and the demons, but of the Jews even the last/least looks upon the God over all alone; and well at any rate, as far as this goes, they pride themselves and turn away from the fellowship of the others as polluted and impious. And would that it had not been sinned by them, transgressing the law, and first having killed 'the prophets' and later also having plotted against Jesus; so that we might have a pattern of a heavenly city, which Plato too sought to sketch, but I do not know if he was able so much as Moses was strong and those after him, nurturing 'a chosen race' and 'a holy nation' and one dedicated to God, in words pure from all superstition.

pass_b_english: As for the rule that one who holds the same beliefs may not be kept a slave for more than six years (Exodus 21:2; Deuteronomy 15:12), what need is there to say how reasonable it is, and how it wrongs neither the master nor the slave? So the Jews would not guard their own law on the same grounds as the other nations. For it would be blameworthy in them, and would bring on them a charge of being blind to the superiority of their laws, if they thought these laws had been written in the same way as the others that the nations have.

And even if Celsus does not like it, the Jews do know something wiser, not only than the multitude, but also than those who are thought to be philosophers. For the philosophers, after their solemn discourses in philosophy, sink down to idols and demons, whereas even the least of the Jews looks to the God over all, and to him alone. And so far as this goes, they rightly pride themselves and turn away from fellowship with others as defiled and impious.

Would that they had not sinned by breaking the law, first killing “the prophets” and later plotting against Jesus too (1 Thessalonians 2:15)! Then we would have a pattern of a heavenly city, which Plato too sought to sketch (Plato, Republic 592b). Yet I do not know whether he was able to do as much as Moses and those after him achieved, who nurtured “a chosen race” and “a holy nation” (1 Peter 2:9; Exodus 19:6), dedicated to God, on words pure of all superstition.
notes: The six-year limit on slavery for a fellow Hebrew is Exodus 21:2 and Deuteronomy 15:12 (cf. Jeremiah 34:14); Origen paraphrases, so both are cited as allusions. 'τὸν ἀπὸ τῶν αὐτῶν ὁρμώμενον δογμάτων' ('one setting out from the same doctrines') = a fellow member of the same faith, i.e. a fellow Israelite. In this section Origen turns Celsus's own phrases from 5.41 back on him (περιστέλλοιεν τὸν ἴδιον νόμον, μεμπτόν, σοφώτερόν τι εἰδότες, σεμνύνονται, τὴν τῶν ἄλλων κοινωνίαν ἐκτρέπονται); since these are echoes woven into Origen's own sentences rather than fresh quotations, they are not set in quotation marks. The staged text has periods before εἰ νομίζοιεν and before ὅτι οἱ μέν; read as continuations. 'ἀναισθησία' rendered 'being blind to'. 'Killing the prophets' and plotting against Jesus together match 1 Thessalonians 2:15 (τῶν καὶ τὸν κύριον ἀποκτεινάντων Ἰησοῦν καὶ τοὺς προφήτας); cf. Matthew 23:37. 'γένος ἐκλεκτόν' and 'ἔθνος ἅγιον' are from 1 Peter 2:9, which itself draws on Exodus 19:6 (ἔθνος ἅγιον) and Isaiah 43:20 (γένος ἐκλεκτόν). 'A pattern of a heavenly city' that Plato sought to sketch recalls Plato, Republic 9.592b (ἐν οὐρανῷ ἴσως παράδειγμα ἀνάκειται, 'perhaps a pattern is laid up in heaven'), the closing image of Plato's ideal city; the shared terms παράδειγμα and heaven make the reference secure, though Origen may mean the Republic as a whole (διαγράψαι also echoes Republic 500e, the city 'sketched' by painters using the divine pattern). Reviewer: σεμνύνονται rendered 'pride themselves' here and in Celsus's words in 5.41 so the echo shows; 'looks to the God over all, and to him alone' removes the ambiguity of 'the God over all alone'; ὁ ἀπὸ τῶν αὐτῶν ὁρμώμενος δογμάτων rendered 'one who holds the same beliefs' (less stiff than 'comes from').
Pass A: the inline Greek lemma tags were moved out of the gloss into lemmas[] (the gloss was over a quarter Greek); the English gloss is unchanged.
